newsitem.title: USA: PSE&G proposes 100 pct customer choice.
newsitem.headline: PSE&G proposes 100 pct customer choice.

text.p: Public Service Electric and Gas Co's will propose 100 percent customer choice of power suppliers on starting January 1, 1999, in Tuesday's filing with state regulators, Senior Vice President -- Corporate Services and External Affairs Alfred Koeppe said Monday.

The Public Service Enterprise Group subsidiary's plan will allow all customers in all customer classes to begin to register their choice of electric energy supplier on October 1, 1998, he told a news conference.
Those customers choosing a supplier other than PSE&G would be switched to that new supplier beginning January 1, 1999.
That is a full 18 months ahead of the timetable proposed by the state Board of Public Utilities' April 1997 restructuring order, Koeppe noted.

The board proposed that 10 percent of New Jersey ratepayers to select energy suppliers as of October 1998, an additional 10 percent in January 1999, a 15 percent allowance in both April and October of 1999, and a 25 percent increment in both April and July of 2000.
Koppe said those chosing another supplier will receive a credit for the energy portion their electricity costs on their PSE&G bill and a bill for power from the chosen supplier.
The third party supplier's charges may be a separate bill or included on PSE&G's bill, he said, explaining "We would have the ability to provide one bill" if the third party supplier is interested.
Vice President Marketing Fritz Lark said the energy credit would be based on hourly cost of power established by the Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland Interconnection.

Until the proper meters are installed at all the utility's 1.9 million customers, hourly use will be based on a profile developed for each customer group from a 900 meter sample now being installed, Lark said.
Later he told Reuters 500 to 600 of PSE&G's largest customers already have such meters -- built by MetroTech -- installed.
The utility is now installing another 900 MetroTech meters to sample use patterns and establish the needed profiles by the end of 1998, Lark said.

During the seven year transition period, Koeppe said, PSE&G would continue to take responsbility for reliability of generation supplying its distribution system, providing "instant" supplies if any third party supplier fails to deliver electricity.
This power would be delivered at the company's then current price with no penalty, he said.
However, PSE&G President Lawrence Codey said the company is looking at annual choice periods when it comes to voluntary switching of suppliers.
Corporate Rate Counsel Francis Delany said the utility is proposing that divestiture of its generating assets not be discussed until the end of the seven-year transition period.
"At the end of the transition period, (the company) would consider transferring generation to a separate entity within the company," Delany told reporters.

"An important part of being simple and fair in energy deregulation is to avoid customer confusion," said Codey. "A plan that calls for 100 percent customer choice of energy supplier from day one eliminates the need to resort to complex explanations of who is eligible to choose a new supplier and who isn't," he explained.

"We also spoke to our business customers -- both large and small -- who cited the same issue of fairness and the need to avoid any anti-competitive formula," said Codey, "which would allow one manufacturer, or department store chain, or pharmaceutical company to have access to an open competitive market before another."

Codey said meeting a January 1, 1999 target for 100 percent customer choice presents an enormous technical challenge. "We are presently working to design a system that will have the flexibility to do a number of critical tasks."

He added, "Because of the complexity of an hourly electric commodity market -- unlike gas which is priced according to a daily market rate -- deregulating the electric industry is not like any other we've seen -- not telephone, not airlines, not railroads." ((-- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710.))
